To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the most cost-effective strategies for reducing the TB burden in high HIV prevalence countries are improving TB case detection to WHO target levels and improving TB cure rates to WHO levels; that ART for TB+ HIV+ individuals is cost-effective but will require substantial new resources; and that averting one HIV infection for US$250 or less is as cost-effective as the TB strategies.

in high HIV prevalence countries, improving TB case finding and cure rates is the most cost-effective strategy to reduce the burden and cost of TB, and averting new HIV infections will have the greatest impact on reducing the burden and cost from TB in the longer term.

in countries with high prevalence of HIV, the most cost-effective strategies to control tuberculosis are to improve case detection and treatment, to treat TB in people living with HIV, and to prevent TB infection in those who are HIV positive.

the most cost-effective strategies for reducing the TB burden in high HIV prevalence countries include improving case detection, improving cure rates and treating TB in HIV-infected people, and that the cost-effectiveness of these strategies will improve as the cost of ART decreases.

TB and HIV control programmes should focus on increasing case detection and improving treatment outcomes, and that ART should be scaled-up in a manner consistent with available resources and health system capacity.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the most cost-effective strategies for reducing the TB epidemic in high HIV prevalence countries are those that improve TB case detection rates to WHO target, and that improve TB cure rates.
the cost of averting one HIV infection is less than averting one HIV case, which is less than averging one TB case.
the cost of averting a TB death is much less than averting a death due to HIV infection, and the cost of averging a TB infection is less than the cost of averring a HIV infection.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cost per DALYS averted is much lower than the cost of averting HIV infections.

, to be cost-effective, HIV treatment should not be limited to individuals with advanced disease, but should be expanded to individuals with less advanced HIV infection, as well as to individuals with latent TB.

TB case detection and TB cure rates should be improved as soon as possible, and the full potential of antiretroviral drugs should be realized in order to reduce the burden on health systems and to improve the health of the population.
